characters: Bismark: a 14-year-old boy in a slightly crumpled uniform, out of breath, with a school bag over one shoulder.
Linda: a 15-year-old girl prefect in a sash and badge, holding a notebook and a whistle.
Mr Acquah: the housemaster, in a checked shirt and tie, with a calm smile and a mug of tea.
Bismark’s mother: a trader at a small roadside stall at dawn, tying up bunches of onions.

narrationPlan.voice: Bright, cheeky student voices; a steady, fair voice for Mr Acquah
narrationPlan.pace: Lively and quick, like a school corridor, slower at the letter (about 125 words per minute)
notes: Read dialogue with a different voice for each character.
Pause for two seconds at each question activity.
Never rush the last page: let the ending land.

music: Upbeat highlife guitar with school-bell hits; a gentle, warm tune for the letter (placeholder)
culturalNotes: The students and staff are invented. The story shows a day school, an assembly with the national pledge and anthem, and a prefect system.
The letter on page 7 is written in exam-safe informal English: full words, correct spelling, friendly phrases and no slang.
Teachers should adapt the setting to their own school (prefect titles, assembly routines and transport).
reviewQuestions: Is the language right for the stated age band and reading level?
Is anything here inaccurate, stereotyped or unsafe for children?

Check the letter format against the BECE English syllabus and marking scheme: sender’s address and date, “Dear …”, introduction, body, conclusion, and a friendly subscription such as “Yours lovingly” or “Your loving cousin”.
Check the idioms (early bird catches the worm; turn over a new leaf; top of the class) with an English teacher for use in informal letters.
Check that the story does not shame late students and that it does not suggest that work at home is wrong.

teacherGuide.overview: A story about punctuality, fairness and listening. It shows a prefect learning to ask why, and models an exam-safe informal letter at the end.
learningGoals: Explain why asking for reasons matters before judging.
Identify friendly, exam-safe phrases in the letter.
Write a short informal letter using full words and correct spelling.
beforeReading: Ask: have you ever been late for a good reason? How did others react?
whileReading: At page 7, ask learners to underline the phrases that make the letter friendly.
afterReading: Write a letter to a cousin telling about one habit you are improving.
Write the same letter once in chat style and once in exam style, then compare.
discussion: Should a late student always be punished?
How can prefects be fair and firm?
reflection: What is one habit you could change with a good plan?

mathsExtension.task: Bismark leaves home at 5:30 and walks 5 km at 5 km/h. When does he arrive?
Assembly starts at 7:15. He arrives at 6:58. How many minutes early?

support: Give a letter frame with blanks: Dear ___, I hope… I am writing to… Your loving ___, ___.
stretch: Write a short speech a prefect might give at assembly about fairness.

culturalNotes: The students and staff are invented. The story shows a day school, an assembly with the national pledge and anthem, and a prefect system.
The letter on page 7 is written in exam-safe informal English: full words, correct spelling, friendly phrases and no slang.
Teachers should adapt the setting to their own school (prefect titles, assembly routines and transport).
localiseThis: Use your own school’s routines, names and terms; adapt titles such as housemaster or senior prefect.

factCheck.claim: Informal letters use a sender’s address and date at the top, a “Dear…” salutation, an introduction, body, conclusion, and a friendly subscription such as “Yours ever” or “Your loving friend”; contractions such as “won’t” and “can’t” are acceptable in informal letters.
